about: Decisions the main agent made on its own authority, with what it recommended and where each stands. Andrew, 2026-11-11: "just be proactive and do what you need to do; make a decisions.json file with all your decisions and what you recommended and just do things and get blaze to work". A decision here is reversed by Andrew saying so; one that changes a rule also changes tools/agents/rules.ts.

decisions.decision: When memory is short the daemon gives back in one order, cheapest to make again first, each step measured before the next (`blaze_graph::giveback::Planner`): the allocators' freed pages, the stores' pool pages, caches, a front end's values by bytes, and last one checkout's kept front end. Three behaviours change with it. (1) A system memory-pressure event takes the values of every kept front end and no front end whole; before, it dropped every kept front end. (2) The builds under way are asked for a release (`Writer::short`) only when their MIR and inference are in proportion to what is short (at most four times the need and its margin), not on every task held back. (3) The front end of the checkout built last (the floor) is never dropped: a task whose wait only the floor could meet waits for a task to end or starts alone, and when the limit falls under what the daemon holds with only the floor left the daemon says so by name and keeps it.
decisions.why: lane memgive-1112 (claude-fable-5-2). On 2026-11-12 a task that waited for 0.09 GiB made the daemon drop reth's kept front end (about 55 GiB held of a limit of 67.08 GiB) and the next build, a one-line revert, took 195.4 s where it takes 4 to 16 s; the same night three daemons squeezed each other and each pressure event dropped every kept front end. Rule incremental-first: the edit loop is what blaze is judged by, and a front end is the dearest thing the daemon holds. What is given up: under real pressure the daemon keeps up to one front end it would have freed (the ceiling's guard and admission's cap are still the last line), and a large task may start alone, serially, where dropping the floor would have let it run beside others.
decisions.recommended: Yes. Confirm on reth's daemon with the limit lowered in steps (docs/v2/plan/design/memory.md, "Giving memory back"): no `is let go` line and edits in seconds while the footprint is under the limit.

Adoption is four steps, each useful alone: blaze as a drop-in for cargo, a shared store, the hub for agent lanes, the hub's check as a required status.

Until then `blaze new --bstd <PATH>` writes the edition package, `--rust` the plain one, and the lint is `allow` unless asked for. blaze's own workspace allows the lint while cargo builds blaze (D25).

Today a package of the edition names bstd by path into a checkout of blaze, so the default would break `blaze new` + `blaze run` on every installed blaze (the release's install check), and the warning would tell people to move to something they cannot build. Lane bstd-entry-1112; for Andrew to overrule.

decisions.decision: A function's error type is the exact set of failures it may return, checked like effects: the set is an error union (`A | B`, edition change 2, ledger E3), `?` widens a member or a smaller set with no `From` written, a failure the set lacks is an error naming the call, the member and the set, and a `match` covers every member. bstd's errors move onto sets: a kind variant that only holds another error (`FsKind::Stopped`, `HttpKind::Net`, `Refused::Stopped`, ...) becomes a member of the function's set (docs/v2/plan/design/error-sets.md has the list).
decisions.why: Asked for by Andrew, 2026-11-12: bstd's ~30 error types should compose, so that `fn main(cx: &Cx) -> Result<(), E>` works when one function mixes `need_fs()?` (Missing) and `open_dir()?` (FsError) with no glue. The union type and its widening were already on main (E3 parts 1 and 2); what was missing was a set as a generic argument (a parser bug), matching by member, the error's words and the proof.
decisions.recommended: Yes: a set costs what the hand-written enum costs (measured for layout), and each area keeps its own error; the alternative, one named enum per mix of areas with `From` impls, is the pattern the edition removes.
decisions.state: built and tested under cargo on branch bstd-error-sets (parser, matching by member, diagnostics, determinism and layout tests); the bstd port waits for D29; the typed binding `e: T`, the unneeded-member advice and inferred sets are not built

decisions.decision: `blaze::implicit_overflow` (edition group, allow by default) refuses integer `+ - * << >>`, unary `-`, compound forms, value-losing casts and profile-dependent or panicking calls (`pow`, `abs`, `next_power_of_two`, `sum`, `product`, `strict_*`) unless the code writes `checked_*`/`wrapping_*`/`saturating_*`/`overflowing_*`/`try_from` or the reach prover shows the operation fits. The proof treats an operation it can't show fits as fitting from then on, so the verdict is the same with and without overflow checks. `/` and `%` are excluded because their panics are the same in every profile. `blaze-std` and `blaze-mem` deny it once `bstd-fallible-alloc` (D29) lands (docs/v2/plan/design/explicit-overflow.md).
decisions.why: Asked for by Andrew, 2026-11-12: code written by LLMs should say whether arithmetic wraps, checks or saturates, denying plain `+ -` or at least linting for it.

decisions.decision: What build, run, check and test show is blaze's own, not cargo's lines: on a terminal a region redrawn while the build runs and at most one line when it ends (nothing for a run that built nothing); off a terminal `blaze: progress` every 10 s and one `blaze: ok` or `blaze: failed` line of key=value fields. `Compiling`, `Finished`, `Running`, `link:` and the per-unit `generated N warnings` and `could not compile` lines are gone; the JSON messages on stdout are unchanged. A frontier (a row a unit under way with how many wait on it) over a dependency tree or a lane a worker, from frames of recorded builds. docs/terminal.md.
decisions.why: Andrew, 2026-11-12: "can you improve the terminal output too? like `blaze run` could be more like nom + buck2 ... proper TUI thing ... reinvent, super modern"; rule useful-not-parity.
decisions.recommended: Yes. The cost: a tool that reads cargo's human lines from blaze's stderr reads nothing it knows (the harnesses filter `blaze:` lines already and read build-finished), and the `blaze check --fix` hint that the per-unit warning line carried is not said anywhere now.

decisions.decision: A proc-macro call whose session moved on (a stateful crate: jsonrpsee's `proc_macro_crate::CACHE`), or whose crate the store has not seen yet, has known reads when it gives, run once more from the fresh state, exactly what it gave in its session: its unit's record and its crate's image are then kept. A call that gives otherwise from the fresh state (a counter) stays unknown and its unit is made again every build, loudly (`misses` step `unit record`).

What is given up: a macro that is truly order-dependent and happens to give the fresh state's output in one build has that output kept; before, nothing of such a crate was ever kept.
decisions.recommended: Yes; run blaze-macro-eval's tests/kept.rs and corpus.rs (BLAZE_MACRO_CORPUS) before it lands.

decisions.decision: A build script's run that read what can't be traced (the clock, randomness, the network) and whose script said what reruns it (`rerun-if-changed`, `rerun-if-env-changed`) is kept by cargo's rule and by what it read of its own package; what it read elsewhere (the checkout's other files through `git`, the toolchain's) is no input of it. A traceable run keeps every read, as before, and so does an untraceable one that named nothing.
decisions.why: lane reth-1112: rule useful-not-parity matches cargo where real code depends on it, and reth does: its `reth-node-core` script stamps the build time and asks `git` whether the checkout is dirty, and says in its source that debug builds must not run it again. Traced, it read 2,916 files of the checkout: every build hashed them (13 s of each edit) and every edit ran it again and remade the crates above it. What is given up: such a script is not run again when a file it read outside its package changes (the `-dirty` suffix of a version string goes stale, as under cargo).
decisions.recommended: Yes.

decisions.decision: The fresh core (docs/v2/plan/design/target.md, interface crate crates/blaze-keyed): one process per command answers from records keyed from text before the work, each carrying the read list its work made; on a key miss the read list is checked against the current surfaces and a verified result is filed under the new key byte for byte. No daemon, no query graph, no memory admission; the memo (`RecordsOnly` for one-shot commands, `Resident` for watch and live runs) and the executor (`Local`, or a remote service) are static type parameters of one driver. Records are the unit of sharing: deterministic bytes, namespaced keys (public only for registry archives by checksum and the toolchain), segments as the wire format, signed statements. It supersedes end-state.md and end-state/*.md.

decisions.decision: Records are read-addressed (docs/v2/plan/design/read-addressed.md, proposed by the test-engine session with an outside review). A body, a surface and a unit manifest are found by what their work read: the key says what the record is (its own text and settings), its shape is the set of facts it asked for, and the key, the shape and the facts' digests now give the address of its value. The text-closure keys (blaze-keyed's text.rs, Relax's rules), the reuse path that refiles a record under a new key, and blaze-unitkey's name graph go. Soundness rests on one claim, that a shape holds every fact the work read, guarded by the recording reader, a simulation whose model reads by value, and an audit mode that redoes every hit and compares bytes. Added here to the proposal: a fact a body makes is routed by its owner so an ask is a lookup in the unit's manifest, with the maker settled before its readers; a manifest's chunk is findable by its file's key. Kept from the test-selection work and not replaced by reach digests: a kept test result is addressed by the functions it executed and its outside reads.
decisions.why: A key hit with no check is unsound for real Rust: `a + b`, `?`, `for`, a deref and auto traits look up what the text does not name, and blaze-unitkey (read 2026-11-13) covers none of them; the simulation could not see it because its model's reads were the key's names. A list of implicit lookups would be a patch per missed case, each a silent stale answer (rules 21, 54). It also removes a copy of every reused record and a re-key of every unit above an interface edit.
decisions.recommended: The test-engine session proposed it and an outside reviewer said adopt with changes; the main agent of the port (claude-fable-5-2) agrees and builds it. The owner has not ruled; it is his to reverse.

decisions.decision: How D40 is built. (1) A theorem is an ordinary Rust function marked `#[blaze::theorem]` that returns `bool`; its Lean statement is total correctness (for every argument it returns `true`, and returns). (2) A state machine is proved a step at a time over a well-formedness predicate written in Rust, and one Lean lemma gives every run. (3) A world is a Rust predicate `allows(asked, answer)` with `apply`, not a script of choices and not a kernel model written by hand in Lean. (4) Both Lean packages move from 4.20.0 to 4.35.0. (5) `blaze prove` is its own command; generated models are build outputs, and the tree holds proofs.
decisions.why: claude-fable-5-2, main agent. (1) cargo still builds blaze's crates, so they cannot carry clause syntax, and a property test and a theorem are then one function. decisions.decision: blaze carries a patched copy of rustls 0.23.46 (vendor/rustls; vendor/rustls/SOURCE.md lists the change). The patch is additive, two functions: a TLS 1.3 client session ticket written as bytes (`Tls13ClientSessionValue::to_bytes`) and read back under a config (`ClientConfig::tls13_ticket_from_bytes`). With it a blaze process keeps the tickets its cache origin sent in an owner-only file beside the credentials (`remote-tickets.bin`, mode 0600, none older than seven days), and the next process sends its first anonymous reads of the public cache as 0-RTT early data. Only a GET or HEAD of an immutable, content-addressed `public/` object goes as early data; everything signed stays on HTTP/1.1.
decisions.why: A blaze command is a process that answers and exits, so each one opens its QUIC connection to the cache from cold: without a ticket from an earlier process that is one round trip before the first request leaves. rustls 0.23 cannot hand a ticket to another process (the value's fields are private, its constructor is crate-private, it has no encoding, and it is tied by pointer to the config that received it), so the piece is built where the fields are (rule build-the-missing-piece), as the tree already does for quinn-proto, cranelift and 20 other crates under vendor/.
decisions.recommended: The main agent (claude-fable-5-2) decided it, after raising it with the owner several times without an answer. A patched TLS library is a thing an owner may not want: the owner has not ruled and it is his to reverse. Reversing is deleting vendor/rustls and its `[patch]` line and blaze-http's `Tickets::add` and `fresh` (crates/blaze-http/src/h3/config.rs) with blaze-remote's tickets file; resumption then works inside one process only.

decisions.decision: A sans-IO loop takes its world as one value, and is proved by running it: the retry loop of every blocking wait (`blaze_core::wait::retry::drive`) takes a `Kernel` (its calls and its clock; a clock and a closure are one), a theorem's function gives the real loop a kernel that answers from a list of answers the world (`crates/blaze-core/src/world/blocking.rs`) allows, and its statement for every list is every run. The loop's simulation test and that test's hand-written kernel are deleted (wait/tests.rs), `a_wait_ends_by_its_deadline` being proved in Lean.
decisions.why: The loop read its clock through `&self` beside a closure that moved it, which only a `Cell` can share; the translator has no model of interior mutability and a functional model should not need one. One value needs none, callers of `until` do not change, and the loop the theorem runs is the loop production runs. The world is at least as liberal as the deleted test's kernel (each of its behaviours is an answer the world allows) and allows more: a timeout early with the event still to come, a call that starts after the clock was read.

decisions.decision: Threads that share atomics are modelled as programs over one world (`lean/Blaze/Threads.lean`): a function that reaches an atomic operation is a tree of operations, `blaze_core::world::threads::two(schedule, first, second)` runs two closures one operation at a time in the schedule's order, and a theorem for every schedule is every interleaving. The world's memory is sequentially consistent and it refuses, never approximates, a run it is not the meaning of: orderings weaker than `SeqCst` are accepted only where the run's threads touch one cell (where every memory model is sequentially consistent); weaker orderings over two or more cells are `Error.unmodelled` until the world has views, and `Relaxed` there until it has promises.
decisions.why: The park's simulation test ran an unpark whole between two of the park's atomics, so it never tried a park's step between the unpark's swap and its wake; an exhaustive statement needs both threads as steppable programs. Treating a weaker ordering as `SeqCst` would be a proof about a program blaze does not compile (rule no-fallback); the single-cell rule makes the first slice sound on real code (a park, a once, a flag, a lock word) without the weak world.
decisions.recommended: The main agent (claude-fable-5-2) decided it. The weak world (views, then promises) is objective V17's remainder.

decisions.decision: An output path has one writer: the job's placement (`Jobs`). The code-memory host, which starts dev test binaries and dev runs, writes no file. A program is launched from a path only after its job's placements have ended, with the key the job's record holds for that path; the host starts it only where that key is its image's key, and otherwise the launch fails with a typed error naming the path, the key placed and the key held. There is no fallback write.
decisions.why: claude-fable-5-2, from measurements of #2145's binaries: a `blaze test` that executed tests replaced its test executable every time (a new inode, 168 MB on macOS, 173 MB on Linux, with `built=0`), where an all-cached run and `test --no-run` did not. The cause, read out of the code by a Claude Opus 5.5 lane: two writers of one path, each with its own record of what the path holds (the build's placement in serve/job.rs and `Host::write_executable` in blaze-inproc), so each one's write made the other's record stale and the next build placed the file again. On macOS a sandboxed test's trace holds its own executable's path, so the rewrite after the test began made `Began::moved` refuse every pass: an opted-in package kept nothing. The two writers always wrote the same bytes under the same key.
decisions.recommended: One writer, not two records kept in sync: a record that is told of the other's writes drifts (it compared length and time only), and any new launch site that forgets to tell it brings the rewriting back. The floor of a run that executes tests is to do nothing to its executable; one writer is at the floor.
decisions.state: Built on branch fix-test-place-1114: the code-memory host writes no file, a launch takes the key the job's record holds, a certificate names what its build left at each output and answers only where the record still holds it. Open beside it: after a restart with no certificate the jobs place every output again.

decisions.decision: Which memory a theorem about threads is stated in is said by the theorem, not found by trying: `blaze_core::world::threads::two` runs the sequentially consistent world (which refuses a run it is not the meaning of, D44), and `threads::two_weak` runs the weak world (`lean/Blaze/ThreadsWeak.lean`: views, release and acquire, stale reads by the schedule's pick). A theorem whose code reaches `two_weak` has its statement over `Prog.valueWeak`; one that reaches `two`, over `Prog.value`; one that reaches both is refused. `Prog.valueAny` (run sequentially consistent, and run again weakly where that refuses) goes. The Rust `two_weak` is the Lean weak world's step, operation for operation, on the same scheduled atomics.
decisions.why: The Rust runner cannot do what `valueAny` does without running the theorem's function twice (a stale read changes what the code does next, so a refused run cannot be replayed, only redone), and a run that is redone another way when the first way refuses is the shape rule no-fallback forbids; nor could a reader tell from a theorem's text which world its `for every schedule` ranges over, though a schedule's picks mean different things in the two. Stated in the weak world a theorem is at least as strong (it allows every stale read the orderings allow), so the choice is the author's: the single-cell rule's cheaper proof where it applies, the weak world where the code's orderings are the point (`handoff::Wake`).
decisions.recommended: The main agent (claude-fable-5-2) decided it. Not covered by either world: a relaxed read followed by a non-releasing write of another cell (rule R1, load buffering), which needs promises; `handoff::Claims` has that shape and keeps its model-checked test.

decisions.decision: Code with no daemon reuses blaze's per-function codegen and linker, re-seated on records, as tasks of the one keyed driver. A plan is one instance's describe as a record, named by content (the item, its type arguments, the settings) and filed at the address of what it read. Code is the dev template blob under the template identity `blaze_codegen::kernel` already defines; it keeps no reads of its own, because it is a function of its plan record and the bodies that plan read. A dependency's generic body reaches a plan as a body record holding MIR, made on demand by a body task that runs inference and MIR only (`kind::Steps::Mir`) in the unit that owns the text. The linker's `Image` state is the kept program manifest's payload. `blaze_program::record::InstanceCode`, its four-section placement and `Sink` are deleted; blaze-program keeps the walk and the row rule and implements the driver's `Walker`.
decisions.why: claude-fable-5-2. The owner, 2026-11-14: "when are u going to have full relax mode and delete the old jank stuff ideally we can just go there in one shot with parallel agents". Reading showed blaze-codegen already compiles one instance at a time to a store-kept template with describe records, and blaze-link already patches in place; what tied both to the daemon was a front end over a live database of every crate and linker state held in memory. An edit after a daemon restart cost 104 to 152 s on hello-world because none of that state was a record.
decisions.recommended: Re-seat, do not rewrite: one compile path shared by the daemon's driver and the command (`blaze_codegen::driver::one`), one walk (blaze-program's), one store. Not chosen: a second driver beside the keyed one for code, or a new code record format beside the template.

decisions.decision: A `mod` that a macro call writes is found by the key task from tokens, without expanding anything: every `mod name;` in an item-level macro call's tokens (with a `#[path]` before it, and inline-`mod` nesting), and every `mod name;` in the body of a `macro_rules!` the unit defines at each call of that name, adds each candidate file that exists to the unit's files, whatever cfg the tokens say. A candidate file's read that cannot be answered is deferred and refuses only if the def map uses the file. A module whose file the tokens do not spell is refused by name in the surface task. A snapshot's database has no disk at all (`base_db::Disk`, a token only a database with a disk holds).
decisions.why: claude-fable-5-2. The second real run of `blaze check --no-daemon` was refused on `core` because `core/src/io/io_slice.rs` declares a module inside `cfg_select!`, which the gather skipped, so name resolution read the file from disk outside the key. The census over the real std then listed 83 such files in three crates (libc 56 through its own `cfg_if!` and a `macro_rules!` that writes `mod types;`, compiler_builtins 26, core 1). A key task cannot expand a macro, and keys must be made from text before any work (rules 21, 65).
decisions.recommended: The over-approximation: more files than the def map uses is sound for a key and costs one image per unused arm's file. Not chosen: a late read discovered by the surface task with a second gather, which would make a unit's file set depend on running its name resolution.

decisions.decision: Positions reach a program through span tables that are records: one `BZSPANS2` table per anchor (`SpanTable`, keyed by the tool and the anchor), read-addressed by a fact per file it names (`FactKind::SpanFile`: the file's printed name and image key, answered by the driver from the key task's rows). The link step is given the tables that came or moved and also runs when only tables moved. A plan reads no file's name or text: `file!()` alone is a `Location` the link fills, and a `concat!` holding `file!()` is a recipe (`blaze_codegen::Target::Text`) the link composes.
decisions.why: claude-fable-5-2. Rule 71: positions are item-relative in every key and record and absolute only when printed. A plan's name held `naming_over` of the root files, which is of the machine (rule 25); and with no span tables as records every function with a panic location was refused at the link. The floor for a comment added above an item is that item's span table and one link step, with no plan and no code.
decisions.recommended: Tables as records with file facts; the driver's simulation holds the floor (`a_comment_edit_runs_span_tasks_and_one_link_and_no_plan_or_code`). Known cost, accepted for now: an edit anywhere in a file reruns the span task of every owner in that file, because the file fact's digest is the file image key.

decisions.decision: An item's signature hash names every item its signature refers to by that item's key and hash, not only by its shape: a parameter or return type that becomes another nominal type of the same shape (`Meters(u32)` to `Feet(u32)`, `PhantomData<A>` to `PhantomData<B>`, a return type with its own impls) moves the signature hash of the function, and with it every stored inference, MIR and borrow-check entry that read the function's signature. The interface, code and layout hashes stay name-free. The store's read rules name the queries that run today (`::served`, `::lowered`), and a test fails when a tracked query a step reads is named by no rule.
decisions.why: claude-fable-5-2, from a finding confirmed end to end on main: a caller's stored inference and MIR were served stale after its callee's parameter or return type changed to another nominal type of the same shape, because the signature hash was of shapes alone. Found beside it: since commit f25aa5be3c (2026-11-13) main's daemon kept no body entry and no goal at all, because the read rules named `XSignature::kept` while the queries had become `::served` and `::lowered`, and five more tracked queries had no rule (`check_relative_bodies`, `generic_params_attr_flags`, `runtime_mir_body_for_coroutine_query`, `slots`, `expanded_item_key`). So the hole was masked on main by a store that kept nothing; the repair without the keyed hash would have opened it.
decisions.recommended: The keyed signature hash and the store repair land together, never the repair alone. The narrowing a Claude Opus 5.5 lane proposed, accepted after tracing the cross-crate case by reading: only the signature hash is keyed. A dependent unit's key holds its dependency's interface as text (signatures as written), which moves with the rename, and `Fact::Signature` is valued by the keyed signature hash, so nothing that validates a dependent rests on a name-free hash of a signature. decisions.decision: Build scripts in check mode. (1) A `git` spawn is answered by blaze from the checkout, read-only, by a small table like the rustc probe table: `rev-parse HEAD` (long and short), the branch, `--version` with a stated fixed string; whether the tree is dirty only if a script asks and only if cheap, else refused by name; the files read join the record's read list, so a new commit reruns exactly those scripts; anything else is the typed 'cannot answer yet' naming the question. The clock stays fixed: a build timestamp is the fixed instant. (2) Other tool spawns (perl, sh configure, pkg-config) are deferred like the C compiler: recorded as requests, the script continued; a script that needs their output to print what check reads cannot produce outputs in check mode, with the tool named. (3) Bindgen at build time (libproc, librocksdb-sys with bindgen-runtime, reth-mdbx-sys) is not worked around: no pre-generated copies from elsewhere, no native tool outside a sandbox; the option is decided by the coordinator with the owner (docs/v2/plan/design/build-scripts.md).

A `git` answer to a build script is a derived fact with early cutoff. The script's record lists the question and the digest of its answer, not the files behind it; a later command recomputes the fact and reruns the script only when the answer changed (a dirty tree reruns it when the bit flips, not on every edit). Each fact states the cost of recomputing it and its floor. Two sources of truth: (1) the workspace checkout's `.git`: refs, the HEAD commit object (loose zlib, or packed through the pack index and delta resolution, with crates/blaze-git-fetch's code moved to a shared place, not copied) for commit time and `describe`, and `.git/index` for dirty by git's own rule (stat matches the entry, else content hashes to the entry's blob), never by spawning git; (2) a fetched git source: no `.git`; the commit id is the lock's, the tree is exactly that commit's, so it is never dirty and `status --porcelain` prints nothing, `--is-inside-work-tree` is true; `log` needs the commit object, which the fetch record does not keep yet, so it is refused by name until the record has a field for it (main changes the record). `describe --tags` walks history within a stated cap of commits read, a typed refusal past it, and is a typed refusal on a fetched source (depth 1, no tags). Refined 2026-11-16 05:50: a fetched git source is by construction a shallow, tagless checkout of the locked commit, and every question about it is answered as git answers in that state: inside a work tree, `rev-parse HEAD` the lock's id, `status --porcelain` empty, `describe --always` the commit's first 7 hex digits (no tag reachable; git's automatic abbreviation, minimum 7), `describe` without `--always` git's `No names found` failure, `log -1` git's failure and a named gap until the fetch record keeps the commit object. This differs from what a full clone with tags would print; it is the truthful answer for what blaze fetched, and it is deterministic. docs/v2/plan/design/build-scripts.md.

decisions.decision: Lexical lookup during expansion-time name resolution. A path's first segment `n` that misses in an inner scope goes outward: the module, then the extern prelude, then the standard prelude, then the built-in types. If the inner scope can still grow by expansion only (unexpanded macro calls in that module; for the extern prelude, unexpanded calls at the crate root), the lookup uses the outer binding; if an expansion that does not enclose the use later writes `n` into the inner scope, that is an ambiguity error at the new definition, in every completion order; written by an enclosing expansion, the inner binding wins; with no outer binding, the inner is used when it appears. A pending glob or named import into the inner scope is not growth by expansion: the lookup waits for it, and a glob candidate beside an outer candidate is an ambiguity (the Reference, glob-vs-outer). An extern-prelude name from the unit's dependencies is final: a macro-written root `extern crate X as n;` may add a name, never replace one (an error). Rules R6 to R8 of docs/v2/plan/design/bottom.md section 6, "Name resolution: the rules (2026-11-16)"; fixtures in crates/blaze-scope/src/tests/name_rules.rs.
decisions.why: The Reference states only the principle (a name "must resolve to the same definition regardless of the order in which macros are expanded and imports are resolved") and not which scope a lookup may take while an inner scope is still open. Taking the outer binding while only expansion can add to the inner scope keeps the solver from stalling on every unexpanded call, and the error at a later conflicting definition keeps the answer independent of order; waiting on pending imports keeps a glob from silently changing a meaning already used.
decisions.recommended: Hold the fast solver and the reference solver to the fixtures r6a to r8b in every completion order; a fixture the fast solver fails stays listed by name in `KNOWN` there until fixed.

decisions.decision: A glob candidate and an outer candidate (extern prelude, standard prelude) for an import's or a macro call's first segment that are the SAME definition, after following re-exports, are one candidate: no glob-vs-outer ambiguity, the name resolves to that definition. Different definitions are the Reference's glob-vs-outer ambiguity.
decisions.why: The Reference's glob-vs-outer sentence forbids resolving through a glob "when there is another candidate available in an outer scope" and does not say whether the same item counts as another. Its glob-vs-glob text allows two globs of "the same item (following reexports)", and its stability principle asks only that a name "resolve to the same definition regardless of the order": with one definition every order gives the same answer, so nothing is gained by an error.

decisions.decision: A crate version that switches its own procedural-macro support off on the sandbox's target is corrected by blaze, by a visible table, and not worked around in any project. The macro world stays one truthful target (wasm32-wasip1) for every crate in it. blaze carries a table of source corrections as data in the repository: the crate, the version requirement, the cfg predicate to replace and what replaces it, the reason, the upstream link. A correction is applied by syntax to the crate's fetched and verified source and yields a derived source record keyed by the source's digest and the row's digest; every reader (the interim macro builder, the names library, expansion) reads the corrected record, and a build names each correction it used. First row: synstructure 0.13 (src/lib.rs and src/macros.rs), where `extern crate proc_macro`, `decl_derive!` and `decl_attribute!` sit under `not(all(target_arch = "wasm32", any(target_os = "unknown", target_os = "wasi")))`: that predicate is replaced by one that holds.

decisions.decision: The program's entry, in two stages with the end state fixed now. END STATE: the module blaze appends to a program's root (`__blaze_entry`) is ONE constant text, `std::guest::start_with(table, crate::main)`, and which roots `main` takes is decided by the type checker through a library trait in bstd (`entry::Main<Roots>`, implemented for functions of the four shapes the rule `entry-takes-roots` allows: none, `&Cx`, `Io`, `&Cx` then `Io`); a `main` of any other shape has no impl and the finding names the rule at `main`'s signature. Nothing about `main`'s types is read before names resolve, and the appended text is the same for every program, so the root's key changes only with the user's own text. INTERIM, until the checker and the code builder pass the end state's fixture (a generic function over a function item with the marker inferred, and the call of a function item through `FnOnce`): four constant texts, chosen from the OUTLINE of the root's `fn main` alone: no parameter; one parameter whose written type is a reference (`&Cx`); one that is not (`Io`); two (`&Cx`, `Io`); more is refused by the rule's name. A wrong parameter type is then a mismatch inside the appended module, reported at `main`'s parameter with the rule's name. In both stages nothing is appended when the root's outline already holds a function exported as `bstd_hosted_start` or `main`; one written by a macro beside the appended one is the typed error naming both.

Choosing by resolved type would need a second resolution of the root crate; choosing by the text of a type is a text match that an alias breaks. A marker trait moves the choice into the type checker with no compiler rule at all (library over language, rule 32) and gives the error a home. It needs function items against `Fn` bounds, marker inference across four impls and a generic instance over a function item in the builder: all needed by real code anyway, none ready today, and the owner's hello world should not wait on them: the interim reads only the shape of `main` from the outline, which the rule makes exact (the one-parameter forms differ in being a reference or not).

decisions.decision: `include_str!`, `include_bytes!` and `include!` follow Rust: the path is relative to the file that writes the call and may leave the package. What bounds it is where the unit's source came from. A workspace member may read any file under the workspace's source root: the root of the version-control checkout that holds the workspace, or the workspace's own root when there is none. A fetched unit may read under its fetched root: the whole checkout for a git source, the package for a registry one. A unit's build-script outputs are read through the script's record as before. Every such read is a tracked input: named in the read list of exactly the body or item that holds the call, by a path relative to its root and with the content's digest (a record is valid by its key, or else by its read list checked against today's facts), so an edit of the file rebuilds only what includes it. A path that leaves the bound is a typed refusal naming the call, the path and this decision; an opt-in for it is not designed until a real project needs one.
decisions.why: tempo reads `../../crates/chainspec/src/genesis/*.json` from another member of its workspace (11 calls), which the package-only rule refused and Rust accepts. The package is the wrong bound for a member: a workspace is one source tree. The source root is the right one: inside it every read can be named without the machine in a key (rule 25) and shipped to a remote worker with the rest of the tree; outside it neither holds, and a fetched package reading beside itself would read files nobody fetched or verified. This is the one place blaze is narrower than the pinned compiler here, by choice, and the refusal says so.

decisions.decision: Borrow and move checking on the rebuilt path, so `blaze check` is a whole check. (1) ONE mid-level form per body, the FLOW: a control-flow graph over places with moves, borrows, reborrows, drops, storage ends and calls, every node with an item-relative range; made once from the typed body, a record keyed like the body's check; the move check, the borrow check and (after the switch) the code builder's drop elaboration read it, so place analysis has one home. (2) The type checker stays lifetime-erased. Signatures gain a lifetime part in their head records (lifetime parameters, where each occurs, outlives bounds; variance per type as a record). The borrow check relates types again over the flow with a fresh origin at every reference position, as constraints between origins at points. (3) The analysis is loans-in-scope by reachability over those constraints and the graph, location-sensitive, in two tiers: a linear location-insensitive pass that accepts almost every body, and the precise pass only for a body the first one cannot accept. A finding is raised exactly when a live loan is invalidated, a moved place is used, or a place is moved out of a borrow. Every program the pinned compiler's borrow checker accepts is accepted; sound programs it refuses (the cursor pattern) may be accepted; none of its soundness holes are. (4) Per body: its record holds the findings and a proof value the code builder takes; it reads only the body's flow and the heads of what the body names, so an edit rechecks one body. (5) `check` says what it checked: until this stage is in the command its summary reads incomplete and its exit status is not 0.
decisions.why: The rebuilt path has no borrow or move check at all, and the owner asked that `blaze check` be a proper check. The rules are not in the Reference in executable form: the sources are RFC 2094 (non-lexical lifetimes), RFC 2025 (two-phase borrows) and the Polonius formulation; expectations in tests are stated from those rules, never taken from a compiler's output. A separate flow form is what makes the checks and drop elaboration agree by construction and gives the verified-compiler goal (rule 57) the one semantics to state; relating types again with origins is what an erased type checker requires and keeps lifetimes out of every type-check key. Two tiers keep the common case linear.
decisions.recommended: Interfaces first (rule 79): one small crate with the flow's types, the constraint and loan state machines and a simulation over hand-built graphs with planted bugs, before any body is lowered to it; then the lowering from the typed body, then real bodies from the census.

decisions.decision: What the type checker asks the front end for is a RECORD, self-contained and read in place; the front end's one in-memory store with one shared type table goes. (1) A head record (a signature, a trait's definition, an impl's header, a predicate list) carries its own small table of exactly the terms it reaches; the checker converts the record it asked for and nothing else, so an answer costs the record's size, never the crate's. (2) An impl's header does not build its members: each member's signature is its own record, asked when a body names it. (3) The impl index (which impls of a trait exist for which shape of type) is records too: one per crate, keyed by that crate's impl headers' text, sorted by (trait, shape) and searched in place; a lookup reads the buckets of the crates in scope; nothing is rebuilt per command. (4) Records are immutable bytes, so every worker reads them at once: no front-end state is bound to a thread; what a task mutates lives in its own frame. (5) They are ordinary records of the driver's store: found by key after a restart, shared across projects through the machine store when their key holds nothing of a project (the toolchain's and registry crates' heads), and fetched from an origin: the standard library arrives with its signatures built. Two stages: FIRST, inside today's code, the three measured costs are removed where they stand (the checker converts only the nodes an answer reaches; the index is built once and kept; member signatures on demand), with counters for rounds, questions and conversions; THEN the store moves into records behind the same world interface, with the body census and the order test as its referee.
decisions.why: Measured on a release build with the real world (port27/speed-1116: bstd.txt, alloc.txt, core.txt; 2026-11-16, a loaded machine): bodies type-check at 26 to 106 a second cold and 63 to 154 warm on one thread, against a floor of 71,747 a second with no world: 470 to 2,800 times slower. Three causes are named with their own numbers: every answer hands the checker the whole shared table (the same warm body: 72 microseconds over its own 28 nodes, 4,178 over the crate's 4,252); the impl index is rebuilt from every impl header on a command's first question (193 to 307 ms, nearly all of a small body's cold check); an impl's header builds every member's signature (a median bstd body pulls in 589 heads, 461 of them functions). The store's types are also bound to one thread, so 18 workers each resolved their own names (600 MB and 4 to 7 s each). None of this is inherent: it is the store's shape, and it is the opposite of the design's first line (everything kept is a record, written once, read in place).
decisions.recommended: Stage one now, in the checker's and the heads lanes' files, each change quoted before and after with crates/blaze-ladder/examples/check_speed.rs on bstd. Stage two as its own lane once the census-driven fixes of this morning have settled, interfaces first.

decisions.decision: One HTTP client, and it is bstd's. The tree has ONE HTTP/1.1 parser (crates/blaze-h1: sans-IO, no_std, on blaze-own) and THREE drivers over it: crates/blaze-h1-net (on bstd's `Net`; ranges and a redirect policy; nothing called it), bstd's `Http::over` (crates/blaze-std/src/requests.rs: on `Net`; no ranges, no redirects) and crates/blaze-http's `Client` with its own driver (a pool, gzip, proxies, TLS through rustls: it leaves bstd's effect layer by starting its own thread with its own native driver and by reading the environment for proxies; crate fetching goes through it). The one home is bstd's `Http`: a program on bstd and blaze's own tools (the shared cache's origin, crate fetching) use the same client through `Net`. It gains what the other two have: the range check against the request (`Response::ranged`), size limits before a body is read, a redirect policy that a caller may set to refuse, deadlines on every wait, then TLS as a sans-IO layer between `Net`'s stream and the parser with the roots from `Net::roots`, then a connection pool. blaze-h1-net is folded in and deleted; blaze-http's HTTP/1.1 client, its thread and its environment read are deleted when crate fetching has moved; a proxy is a value handed to the client by the command's start, never read from the environment inside it. HTTP/3 stays in blaze-http behind its feature until it gets the same treatment on `Net`'s datagrams. blaze-remote's `http.rs` and `http3.rs` bucket readers are not reachable from the command (its `bucket` feature is off) and go with the old store.
decisions.why: The owner: "i thought we already had sans io http/1,2,3 so make sure we are just doing things properly", and "make sure everything is using bstd as base". The survey (docs/v2/plan/design/remote-read.md, "HTTP in the tree", with files and lines) shows the parser is already one and sans-IO; what is triplicated is the driving, and the richest driver is the one outside the effect layer, so crate fetching is neither simulated nor crash-tested. Putting the client in bstd makes the standard library the base it is meant to be, gives the simulation one client to run (its begin/finish split is what lets a simulated server and a client interleave: the stand-alone driver's test could not), and removes a thread and an ambient read (rule 75).
decisions.recommended: Stage one: bstd's `Http` gains ranges, limits, the redirect policy and deadlines from blaze-h1 and blaze-h1-net; the shared cache's HTTP origin is an adapter over it; the simulated servers (pieces, a stall, an early close, a wrong range, a wrong length, a longer body, a redirect, a 404) are each refused by name; measured against a local server. Stage two: TLS and the pool; crate fetching moves; the two other drivers are deleted.

decisions.decision: The concurrent map takes its lock as a type parameter, and blaze-core gives it one. blaze-hash's shared map (shared.rs) names no lock of its own: its per-shard writer lock is a type parameter bounded by a small raw-lock trait that blaze-hash defines. blaze-core, which sits above blaze-hash and owns the tree's one blocking lock (`blaze_core::lock`: named, with a deadline and a span), instantiates the map with it and exports the alias every user names; a `.clippy.toml` ban keeps other crates from instantiating it with any other lock. The interleaving tests instantiate it with blaze-check's lock.

A data structure below with its policy passed in from above is the shape the allocator already has (rule 75) and is rule 78's strategy as a type parameter at one seam. Moving the map up into blaze-core would put a collection in the effect layer; a spin lock would be an unbounded wait under preemption.

decisions.decision: Build scripts that need a C toolchain run NATIVE inside the operating system's sandbox, with blaze's own pinned clang. A build script whose dependency closure holds a crate that starts a compiler or loads libclang (`cc`, `cmake`, `bindgen` / `clang-sys`, and the rest of that class in build-scripts.md's table) cannot run as wasm: WASI has no process to start and no library to load. Such a script is built for the host and run confined (no network, writes only under its `OUT_DIR`, reads only its inputs and the pinned toolchain), and the only compiler it can see is a clang and libclang that blaze fetches by digest to its own shelf. The choice is made from the script's dependencies before it runs and is part of its key: never a second try after a wasm failure. Every other build script, and every procedural macro, stays wasm in Wasmtime.
decisions.why: The owner, 2026-11-16, asked whether to allow a pinned native clang inside the OS sandbox: "ok sure use our pinned native clang maybe inside sandbox since we fork llvm idk  in teh sandbox". 126 units of tempo wait on build scripts that run bindgen (librocksdb-sys, reth-mdbx-sys, libproc), and the same class compiles C and C++ with `cc`: tempo cannot fully build without it. Rule 9 asks for a sandbox, not for wasm; rule 10's wasm is for procedural macros. The machine's own clang is never used: it is not a keyed input.

decisions.decision:
Every finding has an id, two views and a fix that can be applied by id. (1) THE ID is derived from what the finding IS, never from where it happens to print: a digest of the item it sits in, its code and its item-relative range, shown as a short lowercase prefix (five characters of an alphabet without look-alikes; longer only when two findings of one run share a prefix). Because positions are item-relative (rule 71), an edit elsewhere in the file does not change the id. (2) TWO VIEWS of the same records, chosen by `--view person|agent|json`: `person` is the drawn diagnostic; `agent` is one or two plain lines per finding with nothing decorative: the id, the code, `file:line:col`, the message, then the fix as an exact edit with its reason, and a last line that counts and names the command; `json` is the same fields as data (and the agent API carries them in CBOR, rule 33). Default: `person` when the output is a terminal, `agent` when it is not (a pipe, a file, a tool call), so an LLM that runs the command gets the compact view without knowing a flag. (3) `blaze check --fix <selector>...`: a selector is an id or any unique prefix of one (so `e7*` is just `e7`), a code (`E0425`: every finding of that code), a path, or `all`. Fixes are applied as one transaction: a fix whose finding is no longer current (the text under it changed) is refused by name, two fixes that overlap are refused naming both, and after applying, the check runs again and prints what is left. The agent view, exactly, for the owner's example:
e7k2q  error[E0425]  src/main.rs:1:37  cannot find value `c` in this scope
       fix: replace `c` with `b` (1:37-1:38): `b` is in scope, is a `u32`, and is never used
1 error, 1 fix: blaze check --fix e7k2q
decisions.why: The owner, 2026-11-16, looking at the error card on the website: "all errors hsould maybe have an llm viedw like [the card] this should have an llm view and have an id and u can blaze check --fix {id}* as  well or someting idk", then "or just use what makes smot sense". A finding is already a record with an item-relative range (rule 81) and, since today, a fix stored as data (ranges, no strings): the id, the views and `--fix` are three readers of that record. Most commands today are run by agents; a view made for them costs a few lines and saves them reading art meant for eyes.
decisions.recommended: The driver lane: ids on every finding the command prints today (syntax, unresolved imports) and on the checker's fixes; the three views with golden tests; `--fix` with its refusals proven in the simulation; the website's error card shows both views.

decisions.decision: A coroutine is split by a pass over LIR, not by hooks in the builder's walk. The builder builds an async body as an ORDINARY function whose `.await` points end in a `suspend` terminator with two successors: `resume` (where the poll loop continues) and `cancel` (a block that runs the drops of what is in scope there, emitted by the builder's own scope code exactly as it emits a `return`'s exit). One LIR pass then: computes which stack slots and values are live across any suspend, lays out the state (upvars, those slots, spilled values, drop flags, the tag), rewrites every access to a moved slot into a field of the state through the pinned self pointer, spills and reloads values that cross a suspend, and emits two functions: `poll` (a head switch on the tag into the resume blocks; `Pending` returned at each suspend after the tag is stored) and the state's drop glue (a switch on the tag into the cancel blocks). The proven transform in crates/blaze-coroutine (its IR, liveness, layout, and its two-interpreter property test with planted bugs) is the model and stays the oracle: the LIR pass is tested the same way, on LIR.
decisions.why: The adapter writer found that homes for named bindings alone are unsound: the walk keeps temporaries in stack slots (`temp()` and ten direct slot sites), so a reference into a temporary dangles after the first Pending, and cached SSA values do not dominate a resume block. Putting the whole frame in the state through hooks would need a hook in every expression form of a 240 KiB walk that eight writers edit; a CFG pass needs none, sees every slot and value, and is the form liveness is defined on. It is also where the storage-overlap optimisation and later generator forms belong.
decisions.recommended: One writer: the `suspend` terminator in blaze-lir with its verifier rule, the pass with its property test and planted bugs, then the builder's two emit points (async block entry, `.await`). The seam's three answers (`LayoutFacts::coroutine`, `Adts::future_poll`, the held future's type) follow.

decisions.decision: The command's memory follows lifetime: the command's frame holds only what the whole command needs; a task has its own frame, reset per item; what outlives a task is a record; the effect and work lists are not bump-allocated vectors. The class (an infallible push into a bounded frame) is closed by a type with only fallible growth.

decisions.decision: Parallelism and memory of a command (docs/v2/plan/design/parallel.md, "End state"): (1) no fibers for the pipeline's tasks: threads on bstd's work-stealing pool; a task that needs a record another task is writing claims or parks on that key in `blaze_core::claim_table`, or is restarted (its key fixes what it asks); (2) no global interner: a task interns in its own frame and each record carries its own canonical table; (3) a refused allocation is a typed `FrameFull { task, frame, asked, peak, reserve }` failing one job; the class is closed by a type (`A: NeverRefuses`, which a frame is not), reached by a typed handle and a lint first; (4) `claim_table` becomes the hashed core of bstd's `Flight` (one home for single flight); (5) the claim table is sized to twice the keys the request names; (6) the pieces that make heads frozen and `Sync` and put bodies on the pool go to the records writer after the records switch lands.
decisions.recommended: The architect's thirteen pieces in its order; pieces 1, 3, 7, 13 to the driver's lane, 4 and 8 to the name solver's lane, 5 and 9 to 11 to the records writer.
decisions.why: Measured: the front end runs on one thread (tempo: names 25.8 s, 20,000 bodies in 31.2 s); 18 workers give the names run only 2.3x because `Par::map` has no `Send`/`Sync` bound and every crate's names are leaked and stay live (2.3 GB); the command's one 64 MiB frame takes a path copy per task and a refusal is a panic.
decisions.state: decided by the coordinator on the architect's recommendations; assigned

decisions.decision: What an edit costs (docs/v2/plan/design/read-addressed.md, "End state: what an edit costs"): (1) `.blaze/v2/last` is replaced by one pointer per (tool, request shape) at `.blaze/v2/at/<hex16>`, 8 kept; (2) a file's surface hashes a per-item NAMES digest, not the signature hash, so a type edit re-solves no crate's names; (3) the type checker's read-list answer digest widens from 64 bits to 32 bytes before a read list is kept on disk or shared; (4) the repeat's 27.9 to 37 ms is split by measurement (stats, pointer read, answer pages) before a file-system journal is built. Parked as side work: deleting caches.md and blaze-certify. The outline is rebuilt as one tokenization plus an item-header recogniser (its lane's floor: 136 ms for the toolchain's library against 688 ms today), the old path kept only as the oracle until byte-equal.
decisions.recommended: The architect's ten pieces; 1 to the driver's lane, 2 to a writer in blaze-file-items, 3 written (blaze-typeck replay.rs), 10 to the outline's lane.
decisions.why: Measured on tempo: one `pub fn` edit costs 138.1 ms because `Outline::surface` hashes each item's signature; the impl index is rebuilt on every run (about 190 ms); no body's check result is kept or replayed; two builds of blaze in one checkout knock out each other's `last`.

decisions.decision: `blaze test` (docs/v2/plan/design/test.md, "End state"): (1) one forked process per test from a per-suite zygote, not tests in one process (a kept result must be a function of what the test entered and read; threads would share statics and the environment); (2) a test's result is a record at an address made from its id, its asks (each function entered, each outside read) and their answers; a pass at an equal address is reused; failures always run again; there is no retry: a pass and a failure at one address is a `Flaky` finding; (3) a test that starts a second thread selects by its static reach; (4) defaults: a 60 s deadline per test; doctests and `tests/` run by default; benches only with `--benches`; (5) blaze-run's in-memory `suite::Tests` and blaze-testsel are deleted once the plan, postings and head records are wired.
